cases.holding: The court held that California's dependency scheme satisfies due process even though the detriment findings at review hearings that make a section 366.26 termination hearing possible are made by a preponderance of the evidence, because removal must first be proved by clear and convincing evidence and unfitness is established cumulatively before termination.
cases.quote: We conclude that the standard of proof for termination of parental rights under the child dependency statutes comports with the requirements of due process.

relevance.DEC-03: Supplies the controlling California statement of which dependency findings require clear and convincing proof and which require only a preponderance, the framework an agency's substantiated finding feeds into.
relevance.DEC-05: Describes the sequence from petition through jurisdiction, disposition and review that a filed dependency petition sets in motion, and the burden the agency bears at each step.
relevance.ACT-02: Confirms the agency bears the burden at each review hearing of proving detriment and that reasonable reunification services were offered before court-ordered services can be ended.
relevance.OUT-02: Is the leading California authority on the standard of proof for termination of parental rights and its relationship to Santosky.
relevance.FAIL-01: Sets the standards-of-proof baseline against which a reviewing court measures whether an agency or trial court applied the wrong burden.
relevance.INP-04: Lays out the full statutory path a court-initiated dependency referral follows once jurisdiction is found.

cases.holding: The court held that section 366.26 does not violate due process because Welfare and Institutions Code section 388 gives a parent whose circumstances have changed a means to petition for modification and to seek return of the child before parental rights are terminated.
cases.quote: Section 388 provides the "escape mechanism" that mother maintains must be built into the process to allow the court to consider new information.

relevance.OUT-01: Identifies section 388 as the vehicle by which a parent who has resolved the problems that led to removal can obtain reunification after services have ended.
relevance.ACT-02: Explains that once court-ordered reunification services are terminated the parent's remedy is a changed-circumstances petition, not relitigation of the services order.
relevance.OUT-05: Supplies the mechanism for terminating dependency jurisdiction on changed circumstances.
relevance.FAIL-01: Establishes that a juvenile court may not modify its own prior order except through the section 388 procedure, a common ground of reversal.
relevance.ACT-01: Recognizes changed circumstances and a showing of the child's best interests as the statutory path back to parental custody when services are provided voluntarily or by order.
relevance.INP-04: Confirms the juvenile court's continuing authority to revisit its own orders once a dependency case is open.

cases.holding: The court held that the parental-benefit exception to termination requires the parent to prove regular visitation, a beneficial relationship, and that severing it would be detrimental, and that a parent's continuing struggles with the problems that led to dependency are not a categorical bar to the exception.
cases.quote: What it does not allow is a judgment about the parent's problems to deprive a child of the chance to continue a substantial, positive relationship with the parent.

relevance.OUT-02: Is the controlling California statement of the elements and proof burden for the beneficial parental relationship exception at a section 366.26 hearing.
relevance.OUT-01: Clarifies that a parent's failure to become ready for the child's return is not, by itself, relevant to whether the parental relationship should be preserved.

cases.holding: The court held that the first clause of Welfare and Institutions Code section 300(b)(1) authorizes dependency jurisdiction on a parent's failure or inability to adequately supervise or protect the child without any separate finding that the parent was neglectful, blameworthy or unfit.
cases.quote: As we explain, this history makes clear that the Legislature did not intend to impose a parental fault requirement in the first clause of section 300(b)(1).

relevance.DEC-03: Fixes what an agency must be able to prove to support a neglect allegation, and rejects any added element of parental culpability.
relevance.DEC-05: Governs whether the facts alleged in a petition state a basis for dependency jurisdiction under section 300(b)(1).
relevance.INP-10: Defines the substantive threshold an intake report must meet before escalation to a jurisdictional petition is legally viable.
relevance.OUT-05: Supplies the substantive test a court applies in deciding whether allegations fail and the case must be dismissed.
relevance.DEC-06: Marks the statutory line between families that can be served voluntarily and those over whom the court may assert jurisdiction.

cases.holding: The court held that because the juvenile court has a continuing duty to inquire into a child's Indian status, a parent may challenge an ICWA-inapplicability finding on appeal from a later termination order even though no timely appeal was taken from the earlier order that subsumed the finding.
cases.quote: In sum, a juvenile court has an affirmative and continuing duty in all dependency proceedings to inquire into a child's Indian status.

relevance.INP-11: States the affirmative and continuing ICWA inquiry duty that attaches at the very first dependency hearing and never expires during the case.
relevance.FAIL-01: Establishes that ICWA inquiry error is reviewable on appeal from a later order notwithstanding the usual waiver and timeliness rules.
relevance.DEC-05: Requires the court to address Indian status when the petition is filed and at every hearing thereafter.

cases.holding: The court held that California Rule of Court 5.482(c), which directed juvenile courts to proceed as if a child were an Indian child while a tribal membership application was pending, is invalid as inconsistent with the governing statutes, while rule 5.484(c)(2) is valid.
cases.quote: Rule 5.482(c) is inconsistent with those statutes, and with the Legislature's intent, and thus invalid.

relevance.INP-11: Defines who is and is not an 'Indian child' for California ICWA purposes and rejects a state rule that would extend ICWA protections to children merely eligible for membership.

cases.holding: The court held that an agency's failure to conduct the initial inquiry required by California's ICWA statutes requires conditional reversal of the order terminating parental rights, with a remand directing the agency to complete an adequate, record-documented inquiry.
cases.quote: The conditional reversal rule we adopt today clearly distinguishes between the separate issues of whether an inquiry is adequate and whether inquiry error is harmless.

relevance.INP-11: Is the current controlling California remedy rule for inadequate Cal-ICWA initial inquiry by the child welfare agency.
relevance.FAIL-01: Supplies the remedy — conditional reversal and remand — when an appellate court finds the agency's ICWA inquiry deficient.

cases.holding: The court held that the sibling relationship exception to termination of parental rights focuses on the child being considered for adoption, so a court may reject adoption only if adoption would be detrimental to that child, not merely because adoption would harm a sibling.
cases.quote: We conclude that the court may reject adoption under this sibling relationship provision only if it finds adoption would be detrimental to the child whose welfare is being considered.

relevance.ACT-03: Frames how sibling relationships are weighed when children in foster care are placed and considered for permanency.
relevance.OUT-02: Is the controlling California construction of the sibling relationship exception at a section 366.26 selection and implementation hearing.
relevance.ACT-04: Bears on whether keeping a sibling group together can override an otherwise appropriate permanent placement.

cases.holding: The court held that when a finding was required to be made by clear and convincing evidence, an appellate court reviewing for substantial evidence must ask whether the record contains evidence from which a reasonable factfinder could have made the finding with that heightened degree of certainty.
cases.quote: appellate review of the sufficiency of the evidence in support of a finding requiring clear and convincing proof must account for the level of confidence this standard demands

relevance.FAIL-01: Supplies the appellate standard California courts now apply when reviewing any dependency finding the statute requires to be proved by clear and convincing evidence.
relevance.ACT-03: Governs review of the clear-and-convincing removal finding required by section 361(c) before a child is placed in foster care.
relevance.DEC-04: Governs review of the clear-and-convincing showing an agency must ultimately make to justify a removal it effected on emergency authority.
relevance.OUT-02: Governs review of the clear-and-convincing adoptability finding required before parental rights may be terminated.

cases.holding: The court held that the Anders/Wende prophylactic procedures requiring independent appellate review of the record do not extend to appeals by indigent parents or children from dependency orders, so an appeal supported by no arguable issue may be dismissed as abandoned.
cases.quote: In considering this argument, we must keep in mind that Anders's procedures are indeed "prophylactic," and as such are not applicable, as it were, in and of themselves.

relevance.FAIL-01: Defines what an indigent parent's appointed appellate counsel must do, and what the Court of Appeal need not do, before a dependency appeal can be dismissed.
relevance.OUT-02: Controls the scope of appellate review available to a parent appealing an order terminating parental rights.

cases.holding: The court held that substantial evidence supported the trial court's findings of detriment and parental inadequacy and upheld termination of the father's parental rights, reversing the Court of Appeal's contrary disposition.
cases.quote: We conclude that sufficient evidence supports the trial court's decision to terminate the father's parental rights.

relevance.OUT-02: Illustrates the substantial-evidence review a California appellate court gives to a trial court's detriment and unfitness findings in a termination case.
relevance.FAIL-01: Shows the limits on an appellate court's power to reweigh expert testimony and bonding evidence when reversing a trial court's termination decision.

cases.case_name: B.H. v. County of San Bernardino
cases.holding: The court held that a law enforcement agency's CANRA duty to cross-report a child abuse report it receives to the county child welfare agency is a mandatory duty enforceable under Government Code section 815.6, distinct from the responding officer's separate investigative duties.
cases.quote: These provisions indicate that a law enforcement agency's duty to cross-report the receipt of an initial child abuse or neglect report is separate from its investigative duties.

relevance.INP-01: Is the leading California Supreme Court decision on the mandatory character of CANRA reporting and cross-reporting duties and the consequences of breaching them.
relevance.INP-02: Establishes that a report from any source, once received by a designated agency, triggers the agency's own mandatory cross-reporting duty.
relevance.INP-03: Directly governs the law-enforcement-to-CPS referral: it holds the agency's cross-report duty is mandatory and actionable under Government Code section 815.6.
relevance.INP-06: Confirms that a hotline or 911 call received by a designated agency starts the statutory cross-reporting clock regardless of what the investigating officer later concludes.
relevance.INP-10: Distinguishes the receipt-and-cross-report duty from the discretionary investigative judgment that follows, which is what screening escalation turns on.
relevance.FAIL-04: Arose from a child's death after an unreported 911 call and defines when a county may be liable for the failure.
relevance.OUT-06: Provides the California liability framework for serious injury or death following a failure to relay a child abuse report.
relevance.DEC-01: Shows that the decision not to relay or act on a report is constrained by a mandatory statutory duty, not unreviewable discretion.
relevance.PMC-04: Supplies the private enforcement mechanism available when a fatality review traces the death to an agency's failure to perform a mandatory reporting duty.

cases.holding: The court held that Probate Code section 1516.5, which permits termination of parental rights so that a probate guardian may adopt after two years of guardianship, is facially constitutional and does not require a current finding of parental unfitness.
cases.quote: However, it is settled that a showing of current unfitness is not always necessary when a court terminates parental rights.

relevance.OUT-03: Is the controlling California authority on when a probate guardianship may ripen into adoption and what the parent is constitutionally owed in that process.
relevance.OUT-02: Establishes that California may terminate parental rights on the strength of a long-standing guardianship without a contemporaneous unfitness finding.

cases.holding: The court held that the probate court applied an incorrect legal framework in denying special immigrant juvenile predicate findings, and that a young person's uncontradicted declaration can alone support findings of parental abuse, neglect or abandonment and that return to the home country is not in the child's best interest.
cases.quote: We conclude the probate court applied an incorrect legal framework in ruling on Saul's petition.

relevance.OUT-03: Governs the evidentiary showing required of a guardianship petitioner seeking the state-court predicate findings that unlock federal special immigrant juvenile status.
relevance.OUT-04: Controls SIJ predicate findings for older youth, including nonminors, who need them to stabilize status as they transition out of care.
relevance.INP-05: Addresses a child- or caregiver-initiated petition for protective relief made without any agency substantiation of abuse.

cases.case_name: Jacob B. v. County of Shasta
cases.holding: The court held that the Civil Code section 47(b) litigation privilege barred a damages action based on a county's disclosure of confidential juvenile record information in a letter filed in a family law proceeding, and that the privilege applies even to a claim grounded in the state constitutional right of privacy.
cases.quote: We conclude that the litigation privilege applies even to a constitutionally based privacy cause of action.

relevance.FAIL-06: Marks the outer limit of a private damages remedy when an agency discloses confidential juvenile record information in the course of litigation.
relevance.PMC-05: Shows that California's juvenile confidentiality regime is enforced through section 827 court procedures rather than through tort suits against disclosing agencies.
relevance.PMC-04: Bears on who may obtain confidential juvenile records when reviewing an agency's handling of a case.

cases.case_name: International Federation of Professional & Technical Engineers, Local 21 v. Superior Court
cases.holding: The court held that the names and salaries of individual public employees are subject to disclosure under the California Public Records Act because the public's interest in the information outweighs the employees' privacy interest, and the personnel-file exemption does not shield it.
cases.quote: Balancing these interests, we conclude that disclosure of the salary information at issue in the present case would not constitute an unwarranted invasion of personal privacy.

relevance.PMC-05: Supplies the California balancing test a requester meets to compel disclosure of agency records over a claimed privacy exemption.
relevance.PMC-02: Is the authority for obtaining the payroll and expenditure records that underlie any independent audit of a county child welfare agency.
relevance.PMC-06: Establishes the public-access baseline that makes agency-level data collection and cross-analysis lawful in California.
relevance.FAIL-06: Defines when an agency's refusal to release records is an unlawful withholding rather than a protected exemption.

cases.case_name: City of San Jose v. Superior Court
cases.holding: The court held that writings by public employees concerning the conduct of public business are public records subject to the California Public Records Act even when sent, received or stored on personal accounts or devices.
cases.quote: we hold that a city employee's writings about public business are not excluded from CPRA simply because they have been sent, received, or stored in a personal account.

relevance.PMC-05: Closes the personal-account loophole for anyone seeking child welfare agency records under the California Public Records Act.
relevance.PMC-01: Makes agency communications about CFSR performance and program improvement plans reachable by public records request regardless of the account used.
relevance.PMC-02: Extends records access to the internal communications that reveal how audit and financial findings were handled.
relevance.PMC-03: Supports public access to citizen review panel communications and materials held by agency staff.
relevance.PMC-06: Confirms the lawful availability of the agency communications a cross-jurisdiction analysis depends on.
relevance.FAIL-06: Holds that an agency cannot defeat a disclosure obligation by pointing to where a record happens to be stored.

cases.holding: The court reversed a dispositional removal order because the record did not show by clear and convincing evidence that there were no reasonable means of protecting the child short of removal, and it was not apparent the juvenile court had applied the clear and convincing standard.
cases.quote: Removal on any ground not involving parental rejection, abandonment, or institutionalization requires a finding that there are no reasonable means of protecting the child without depriving the parent of custody.

relevance.ACT-03: States the clear-and-convincing, no-reasonable-means finding California requires before a child may be placed out of the home at disposition.
relevance.DEC-04: Supplies the standard the juvenile court applies when it reviews an emergency removal at the dispositional hearing.
relevance.INP-12: Sets the substantive limit on continued protective custody once the matter reaches the dependency court.
relevance.FAIL-02: Is the California analogue to the federal rule that removal requires more than a general safety concern.
relevance.ACT-05: Supports use of less drastic protective measures, including orders removing the offending adult, in place of removing the child.

cases.holding: The court reversed removal orders because the agency's report contained no discussion of reasonable efforts to prevent removal and the juvenile court made no statement of facts supporting removal, while ample less drastic alternatives existed.
cases.quote: Ample evidence existed of "reasonable means" to protect Ashly and Cristina in their home.

relevance.ACT-03: Holds that the agency must actually document its reasonable efforts to avoid removal and the court must state the facts supporting removal.
relevance.ACT-02: Illustrates the in-home services and orders that count as reasonable means of protecting a child short of removal.
relevance.FAIL-01: Is a leading California example of reversal for the agency's and court's failure to make the required reasonable-efforts findings.

cases.case_name: Gonzalez v. Santa Clara County Department of Social Services
cases.holding: The court held that a substantiated finding of physical abuse based on parental discipline could not stand where the agency failed to consider whether the discipline was reasonable and necessary, and that the reviewing court applies the substantial evidence rule to the agency's findings.
cases.quote: Rather the court is required to apply the substantial evidence rule, under which the trial court's findings must be upheld if supported by substantial evidence.

relevance.DEC-03: Governs the standard a California court applies in reviewing a substantiated child abuse finding and the parental-discipline defense to it.
relevance.FAIL-01: Supplies the California standard of review for a challenge to an agency's substantiation of an abuse report.

cases.holding: The court held that where relatives requested placement at the outset and the agency never conducted the assessment section 361.3 requires, the juvenile court erred by applying the caregiver adoption preference instead of the relative placement preference on the relatives' section 388 petition.
cases.quote: We accept the Agency's concession the juvenile court erred when it applied the caregiver adoption preference at the section 388 hearing.

relevance.ACT-04: Holds that an agency's failure to timely assess a requesting relative under section 361.3 cannot be cured by later invoking the caregiver preference.
relevance.OUT-03: Protects a relative's statutory path to placement and kinship permanency when the agency has delayed the required home assessment.

cases.holding: The court held that the juvenile court erred in terminating dependency jurisdiction over a nonminor dependent because the order rested on a misunderstanding of the law governing extended foster care eligibility and acceptable supervised independent living placements.
cases.quote: We agree the court erred because it based its order on a misunderstanding of the law.

relevance.OUT-04: Directly governs termination of juvenile court jurisdiction over a nonminor dependent in California's extended foster care program.

cases.holding: The court held that substantial evidence supported the juvenile court's finding by clear and convincing evidence that active efforts had been made, and that under California law 'active efforts' under ICWA and 'reasonable services' under section 366.21(g)(1) do not differ significantly.
cases.quote: Under California law, there is no significant difference between "active efforts" required by ICWA and "reasonable services" required in both ICWA and non-ICWA cases under section 366.21, subdivision (g)(1).

relevance.INP-11: Defines the content of the ICWA 'active efforts' obligation as California courts apply it and the standard of review for that finding.
relevance.ACT-02: Equates the active-efforts showing in ICWA cases with the reasonable-services showing required in every California dependency case.
relevance.OUT-01: Governs the finding a court must make about the adequacy of services before reunification may be ended in an Indian child's case.

cases.case_name: San Joaquin County Human Services Agency v. Marcus W.
cases.holding: The court reversed an order compelling a dependent minor to undergo periodic blood transfusions over his religious objection, holding the juvenile court lacked jurisdiction to issue the order because the procedural requirements of Welfare and Institutions Code section 369 were not satisfied.
cases.quote: We conclude the juvenile court lacked jurisdiction to issue the order because the requirements of Welfare and Institutions Code section 369 were not met.

relevance.ACT-06: Is the California authority on the statutory procedure a court must follow before authorizing medical treatment for a dependent child over the objection of the child or parent.
relevance.INP-07: Shows the limits on agency and court authority to compel medical intervention disclosed or recommended in a healthcare setting.

cases.holding: The court held that a restraining order issued by the juvenile court under Welfare and Institutions Code section 213.5 may be renewed by the family court after dependency jurisdiction ends, because section 213.5 orders are issued under the same standards as Domestic Violence Prevention Act orders.
cases.quote: In 2012, Welfare and Institutions Code section 213.5 was amended so that the juvenile court could issue DVROs under the same standards provided for in the DVPA.

relevance.ACT-05: Is the California authority on the standard for juvenile court protective orders under section 213.5 and their continuity after the dependency case closes.

cases.holding: The court held that the absolute immunity Penal Code section 11172(a) confers on mandated reporters barred the parents' claims against the physician and hospital arising from a report of suspected child abuse, notwithstanding the loss of any civil remedy.
cases.quote: The Legislature's solution in bestowing absolute immunity to the enumerated professionals was an attempt to remove one of the largest impediments to reporting

relevance.INP-01: States the rationale and reach of California's absolute statutory immunity for mandated reporters under Penal Code section 11172.
relevance.INP-02: Explains why California extends broad reporting immunity, the policy that also shapes good-faith protection for voluntary reporters.
relevance.INP-06: Underpins the good-faith protection that makes anonymous and confidential hotline reporting workable in California.
relevance.INP-07: Applies the immunity directly to medical practitioners and their employers reporting suspected abuse discovered in treatment.

cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit
cases.holding: Sitting en banc, the court held that officials ordinarily must obtain prior judicial authorization before removing a child from parental custody, and that a genuine dispute existed as to whether the newborn here was in imminent danger of serious bodily injury such that no warrant was required.
cases.quote: Under the Fourth Amendment, government officials are ordinarily required to obtain prior judicial authorization before removing a child from the custody of her parent.

relevance.DEC-04: Is the controlling en banc Ninth Circuit rule that warrantless emergency removal is lawful only on reasonable cause to believe the child faces imminent danger of serious bodily injury.
relevance.INP-12: Sets the constitutional ceiling on protective custody taken without a court order in California's circuit.
relevance.FAIL-02: Supplies the governing standard for a section 1983 wrongful removal claim in the Ninth Circuit.
relevance.ACT-03: Requires judicial authorization before a child is taken into foster care absent a genuine emergency.
relevance.INP-03: Constrains what law enforcement may do on a referral before a court order issues.
relevance.ACT-05: Confirms that a court order, not unilateral agency action, is the ordinary route to protective intervention.

cases.case_name: Rogers v. County of San Joaquin
cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit
cases.holding: The court held that a California social worker violated the family's Fourth and Fourteenth Amendment rights by removing children without a warrant where the conditions observed presented no imminent risk of serious bodily harm, and denied qualified immunity.
cases.quote: Thus, we hold that, under any view of the facts, the Rogerses' Fourth and Fourteenth Amendment rights were violated when Royal removed the children without a warrant.

relevance.FAIL-02: Is the Ninth Circuit's clearest application of the wrongful-removal rule to a California county social worker, with qualified immunity denied.
relevance.DEC-04: Shows that squalid or neglectful home conditions, without imminent risk of serious bodily harm, do not justify warrantless removal.
relevance.INP-12: Marks the constitutional boundary of emergency protective custody taken by a California social worker.

cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit
cases.holding: The court held that parents and children have a constitutional right to live together free of governmental interference, that children may not be removed without a court order absent reasonable cause to believe of imminent danger of serious bodily injury, and that intrusive medical examinations of children in protective custody may not be conducted without a court order or parental notice and consent.
cases.quote: Parents and children have a well-elaborated constitutional right to live together without governmental interference.

relevance.ACT-06: Is the governing Ninth Circuit authority on examining or treating a child in protective custody without a court order or parental notice and consent.
relevance.FAIL-02: States the familial association right that a removal without exigency or judicial authorization violates.
relevance.DEC-04: Supplies the imminent-danger-of-serious-bodily-injury standard for removal without a court order.
relevance.ACT-03: Governs what may be done to a child once placed in protective custody, including medical examinations.
relevance.INP-07: Limits the forensic medical examination of a child taken into custody on a suspicion of abuse.
relevance.INP-12: Defines the constitutional limits on emergency protective custody and on what follows it.

cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit
cases.holding: The court held that social workers who use perjured testimony and fabricated evidence to secure a child's removal are not protected by absolute or qualified immunity, because absolute immunity covers only quasi-prosecutorial and quasi-judicial functions.
cases.quote: Absolute immunity from private lawsuits covers the official activities of social workers only when they perform quasi-prosecutorial or quasi-judicial functions in juvenile dependency court.

relevance.FAIL-02: Is the leading Ninth Circuit authority that judicial deception by a California social worker to obtain removal is actionable under section 1983.
relevance.FAIL-01: Defines the misconduct — fabricated evidence and perjured testimony — that most often underlies reversal of an agency-obtained order.
relevance.DEC-04: Constrains what an agency may tell a court to obtain authorization for removal.

cases.case_name: Humphries v. County of Los Angeles
cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit
cases.holding: The court held that California's Child Abuse Central Index listing scheme deprives listed persons of a protected liberty interest under the stigma-plus test without adequate procedural due process, because California provided no meaningful process to challenge or remove a listing.
cases.quote: The Humphries have asserted the existence of a sufficient liberty interest under the stigma-plus test, of which they may not be deprived without due process of law.

relevance.DEC-03: Is the controlling circuit authority that a California substantiated finding placed on the Child Abuse Central Index triggers procedural due process protections.
relevance.FAIL-01: Establishes the constitutional defect — no adequate hearing — in California's former CACI listing practice.
relevance.FAIL-05: Supplies the due process framework for challenging a stigmatizing agency listing that restricts employment and licensing.
relevance.OUT-05: Bears on what must happen to a registry listing when allegations are not proven or a case is dismissed.

cases.case_name: Dees v. County of San Diego
cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit
cases.holding: The court reversed judgment as a matter of law for the county on the child's Fourth Amendment and the mother's Fourteenth Amendment seizure claims, holding a jury could find the social worker seized the child by interviewing her at school without a warrant, court order, parental consent, exigency or reasonable suspicion.
cases.quote: We reverse the district court's grant of judgment as a matter of law on L and Sara's respective Fourth and Fourteenth Amendment claims regarding the seizure.

relevance.DEC-02: Is the current Ninth Circuit authority on the authority a California social worker needs before interviewing a child during an investigation.
relevance.INP-08: Directly governs the school-based interview of a suspected child abuse victim without parental consent or a court order.
relevance.INP-10: Constrains the investigative steps an agency may take when it escalates a screened report to an in-person assessment.

cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit
cases.holding: The court held that a mother and child stated a Fourteenth Amendment familial association claim based on judicial deception by a social worker who allegedly made deliberately false statements to obtain a custody order, and that the worker was not entitled to qualified immunity at the pleading stage.
cases.quote: Thus, we conclude that David has successfully stated a claim for violation of her and B.D.'s right to familial association based on judicial deception.

relevance.FAIL-02: Confirms that deliberately false statements used to obtain a removal or custody order are actionable in the Ninth Circuit notwithstanding qualified immunity.
relevance.DEC-02: Constrains how an investigator may characterize investigative findings when seeking court authorization.
relevance.DEC-04: Governs the accuracy an agency owes the court when it seeks authorization to take a child into custody.
relevance.INP-10: Bears on the integrity of the record an agency builds when escalating a report toward court action.

cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit
cases.holding: The court held that a mother and daughter adequately pleaded Fourteenth Amendment familial association claims against officials who participated in removing the child without a warrant or exigency, reversing dismissal as to those defendants while affirming dismissal of the judicial deception claim.
cases.quote: We conclude that certain of Keates's and A.K.'s claims against the defendants who allegedly participated in the interference with familial association withstand the motion to dismiss.

relevance.FAIL-02: Sets out the Ninth Circuit pleading standard for a family's section 1983 claim arising from a removal effected without a warrant or exigency.
relevance.DEC-04: Confirms that the absence of a warrant or genuine exigency exposes each participating official to liability for the removal decision.

cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit
cases.holding: The court held that the case plan and case records provisions of the federal Child Welfare Act, 42 U.S.C. sections 671(a)(16) and 675(1), create rights enforceable by foster children under section 1983, while the guardian ad litem provision does not, and reinstated the children's substantive due process claims arising from harm suffered in state custody.
cases.quote: We conclude that the case plan provisions of the CWA, codified at §§ 671(a)(16) and 675(1), are enforceable through § 1983.

relevance.FAIL-03: Identifies precisely which federal Title IV-E child welfare requirements foster children may enforce in court and which they may not.
relevance.OUT-06: Supplies the Ninth Circuit framework for a foster child's claim arising from serious harm suffered while in agency custody.
relevance.FAIL-04: Establishes the special relationship the state assumes toward children it places in foster care and the duties that flow from it.
relevance.ACT-02: Makes the statutory case plan requirement judicially enforceable by the child it protects.
relevance.ACT-03: Attaches enforceable federal duties of care and record-keeping to a child's foster placement.
relevance.ACT-06: Arose in part from the agency's failure to approve necessary medical treatment for a child in its custody.
relevance.OUT-04: Makes the case plan and records duties that govern a youth's transition out of care judicially enforceable.
relevance.PMC-01: Identifies the federal Title IV-E state plan requirements whose performance CFSR measures and which are privately enforceable.
relevance.INP-05: Bears on what a caregiver or youth may demand of an agency that has assumed responsibility for a child.
relevance.INP-09: Marks which federal child welfare requirements can be enforced in litigation rather than only through federal administrative oversight.

cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit
cases.holding: The court held that a father's asserted procedural due process right to notice of significant changes in his dependent child's care and placement was not clearly established, so the California county officials were entitled to qualified immunity.
cases.quote: We conclude that the defendants are entitled to qualified immunity on these claims and accordingly affirm the grant of summary judgment.

relevance.ACT-03: Addresses what notice a California parent is constitutionally owed when the agency changes a dependent child's placement or care.
relevance.FAIL-06: Shows the limits of a constitutional claim premised on an agency's failure to disclose information to a parent about a child in care.
relevance.OUT-06: Arose from the death of a child in an agency-approved placement and defines the parent's limited federal remedy.

cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: The Court held that New York's fair-preponderance-of-the-evidence standard for permanently terminating parental rights violates the Due Process Clause, and that the State must support its allegations by at least clear and convincing evidence.
cases.quote: Today we hold that the Due Process Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment demands more than this.

relevance.OUT-02: Is the federal constitutional floor for the standard of proof required before parental rights may be permanently terminated.

cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: The Court held that the Adoption Assistance and Child Welfare Act's requirement that states make 'reasonable efforts' to prevent removal and reunify families does not create a right enforceable by beneficiaries under section 1983 or by implied right of action.
cases.quote: We hold that the Act does not create an enforceable right on behalf of respondents.

relevance.FAIL-03: Establishes that federal reasonable-efforts compliance is enforced through the federal funding and review process, not by private suit.
relevance.PMC-01: Confirms that CFSR and the Secretary's funding leverage, not private litigation, are the mechanism for enforcing state plan requirements.
relevance.PMC-02: Confirms that federal financial oversight is the principal remedy for a state's failure to meet Title IV-E requirements.
relevance.PMC-03: Shows why CAPTA-created oversight bodies matter: statutory compliance is largely enforced administratively rather than in court.
relevance.ACT-02: Limits a parent's ability to sue to compel the reasonable efforts a federal statute requires a state to make.
relevance.DEC-06: Leaves the design of front-end alternatives to removal to state discretion under federal plan requirements.
relevance.INP-09: Locates enforcement of federal child welfare standards in federal administrative oversight rather than private litigation.

cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: The Court held that the Equal Protection Clause forbids a court from removing a child from a parent's custody because of the racial composition of the parent's household, even where private biases might expose the child to social stigma.
cases.quote: Classifying persons according to their race is more likely to reflect racial prejudice than legitimate public concerns; the race, not the person, dictates the category.

relevance.FAIL-05: Is the controlling federal authority that race may not drive a custody or placement decision, whatever private prejudices may exist.
relevance.ACT-04: Forbids using the race of a relative caregiver or the racial composition of a household as a placement criterion.
relevance.ACT-03: Bars racial classification as a basis for deciding where a child in state custody is placed.

cases.case_name: DeShaney v. Winnebago County Department of Social Services
cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: The Court held that the Due Process Clause imposes no affirmative obligation on a state to protect a child from private violence, so a county's failure to remove a child it knew was being abused by his father did not violate substantive due process.
cases.quote: But nothing in the language of the Due Process Clause itself requires the State to protect the life, liberty, and property of its citizens against invasion by private actors.

relevance.OUT-06: Sets the federal constitutional baseline for liability when a child is killed or seriously injured while known to the agency but not in its custody.
relevance.FAIL-04: Is the controlling authority limiting substantive due process liability for a child's death under agency supervision short of state custody.
relevance.DEC-01: Establishes that a decision to screen out or close a report, standing alone, does not create federal constitutional liability.
relevance.INP-09: Explains why oversight and fatality review, rather than constitutional litigation, are the principal accountability mechanisms for agency inaction.
relevance.FAIL-03: Confirms that a state's failure to protect a child is generally not remediable as a federal constitutional violation.
relevance.PMC-04: Is the reason fatality review commissions exist: the Constitution supplies no remedy for most agency failures to protect.

cases.case_name: Lassiter v. Department of Social Servs. of Durham Cty.
cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: The Court held that due process does not require appointment of counsel for indigent parents in every parental rights termination proceeding; the trial court must decide case by case, subject to appellate review.
cases.quote: neither can we say that the Constitution requires the appointment of counsel in every parental termination proceeding.

relevance.OUT-02: Sets the federal due process floor for appointment of counsel in termination proceedings, which California exceeds by statute.
relevance.FAIL-01: Frames the case-by-case due process inquiry an appellate court applies when counsel was not appointed below.

cases.case_name: Mississippi Band of Choctaw Indians v. Holyfield
cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: The Court held that 'domicile' under ICWA is a matter of uniform federal law, that children born off-reservation to reservation-domiciled parents were domiciled on the reservation, and that the tribal court therefore had exclusive jurisdiction over their adoption.
cases.quote: One reason for this rule of construction is that federal statutes are generally intended to have uniform nationwide application.

relevance.INP-11: Is the foundational Supreme Court decision on ICWA's exclusive tribal jurisdiction and on reading ICWA's terms as uniform federal law rather than by state definitions.

cases.holding: The court affirmed the Court of Appeal and held that a father's prolonged and egregious sexual abuse of his daughter can be substantial evidence supporting dependency jurisdiction over his sons under section 300(j), even though the sons were never abused and were unaware of their sister's abuse.
cases.quote: We conclude that a father's prolonged and egregious sexual abuse of his own child may provide substantial evidence to support a finding that all his children are juvenile court dependents.

relevance.DEC-03: Is the leading modern California Supreme Court statement of what substantiated abuse of one child proves about the risk to that child's siblings.
relevance.DEC-05: Governs the sufficiency of section 300(j) sibling-risk allegations in a dependency petition and the substantial-evidence review the jurisdictional finding receives.
relevance.INP-10: Tells an agency escalating a report that abuse of one child in the household can justify investigating and petitioning as to every child in it.

cases.holding: The court reversed the Court of Appeal and held that 'substance abuse' under section 300(b)(1)(D) bears its ordinary meaning and needs no medical diagnosis or DSM showing, but rejected the 'tender years' presumption that a substance abuse finding is prima facie evidence of an inability to provide regular care and of a substantial risk of serious physical harm.
cases.quote: Substance abuse, when shown to exist, should not be regarded as automatically amounting to prima facie evidence of the other facts required for dependency jurisdiction.

relevance.DEC-03: Is the current California Supreme Court law on what a parent's substance use does and does not establish when an agency substantiates a neglect allegation.
relevance.DEC-05: Requires an agency filing a section 300(b)(1) petition to plead and prove inability to provide regular care and a substantial risk of serious physical harm, not merely substance abuse.
relevance.DEC-06: Narrows the set of families over whom a court may assert jurisdiction, leaving substance-affected families without proven risk to voluntary or alternative response.

cases.holding: The court held that dependency jurisdiction under section 300(f), which applies where a parent caused another child's death through neglect, may rest on a breach of ordinary care and does not require criminal negligence.
cases.quote: we conclude that section 300(f) does not limit its application to criminal negligence.

relevance.DEC-05: Supplies the California Supreme Court's construction of the section 300(f) ground for filing a petition as to surviving children after a sibling's death.
relevance.OUT-06: Is the California authority linking a child fatality caused by parental neglect to dependency jurisdiction over the surviving children.
relevance.FAIL-04: Defines the degree of fault a child's death must reflect before it carries legal consequences for the surviving siblings' dependency status.

cases.holding: The court held that at a six-month review hearing under section 366.21(e) the juvenile court must assess the likelihood of reunification during the time remaining until the next review hearing, not a fresh six months, and affirmed the termination of reunification services.
cases.quote: That is, the period for which services can be ordered and the period for which the impact of those services is to be prospectively evaluated should be coterminous.

relevance.ACT-02: Is the governing California Supreme Court authority on how the reunification period and the adequacy of court-ordered services are measured at each review hearing.
relevance.OUT-01: Fixes the window within which a parent's prospect of reunification is judged before services may be ended.

cases.holding: The court affirmed the Court of Appeal and held that a finding that reasonable services were not provided in the most recent review period does not itself require extending reunification services past 18 months, while the juvenile court retains discretion under section 352 to continue the hearing and order further services if delay is not contrary to the child's interests.
cases.quote: A court's use of its discretionary authority under section 352 may be particularly appropriate in cases where a parent has never received reasonable services during the reunification stage.

relevance.ACT-02: Is the current California Supreme Court authority on what follows from a finding that court-ordered reunification services were not reasonable.
relevance.OUT-01: Defines the limited circumstances in which a parent may obtain additional time and services to achieve reunification beyond the statutory deadlines.

cases.holding: The court reversed the Court of Appeal and held that a reviewing court may not receive postjudgment evidence outside the appellate record, including unsworn statements of counsel, to reverse an order terminating parental rights, because dependency appeals are governed by the generally applicable rules confining review to the record.
cases.quote: There is no blanket exception to the general rule for juvenile dependency appeals.

relevance.FAIL-01: Controls what a reviewing court may consider when asked to reverse a juvenile court order, and forecloses reversal on evidence never presented below.
relevance.OUT-02: Governs the appellate record and the use of postjudgment developments on review of an order terminating parental rights.

cases.holding: The court held that a juvenile court's error in the procedure used to appoint a guardian ad litem for a parent is trial error subject to harmless error analysis rather than structural error requiring automatic reversal, and was harmless on this record.
cases.quote: If the outcome of a proceeding has not been affected, denial of a right to notice and a hearing may be deemed harmless and reversal is not required.

relevance.FAIL-01: Supplies the prejudice standard that decides most California dependency appeals: procedural error reverses an order only if it affected the outcome.

cases.holding: The court reversed a dismissal and held that a child states a cause of action against a physician and hospital for negligently failing to diagnose battered child syndrome and to report it as Penal Code section 11161 then required, because both the standard of care and proximate cause are questions of fact.
cases.quote: Accordingly, the trial court in the case at bar could not properly rule as a matter of law that the defendants' negligence was not the proximate cause of plaintiff's injuries.

relevance.INP-01: Is the foundational California decision that a mandated reporter's failure to report can itself be actionable negligence, the duty side of the reporting scheme.
relevance.INP-07: Directly governs a physician's obligation in a healthcare encounter to recognize and report the injuries that signal abuse.
relevance.FAIL-04: Establishes that further injury suffered after an unreported abuse presentation may be traced in damages to the failure to report.

cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit
cases.holding: The court held that a social worker and police officer who coerced their way into a family home to investigate an anonymous child abuse report, without a warrant, consent or special exigency, violated clearly established Fourth Amendment rights and were not entitled to qualified immunity.
cases.quote: Under White, appellants' claim, that "a search warrant is not required for home investigatory visits by social workers," is simply not the law.

relevance.DEC-02: Is the governing Ninth Circuit rule that accepting a report for investigation does not authorize entering the family home without a warrant, consent or exigency.
relevance.INP-10: Constrains the home visit that typically follows escalation of a screened report to a formal investigation.
relevance.FAIL-02: Establishes that a coerced, warrantless home entry by a California child welfare investigator is actionable under section 1983.

cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit
cases.holding: The court held that a California county social worker was not entitled to summary judgment on qualified immunity for a warrantless removal, because a jury could find that the child faced no imminent danger of serious bodily injury even though there was probable cause sufficient to obtain a removal warrant.
cases.quote: Nonetheless, imminent danger of future harm is required to show exigency.

relevance.DEC-04: Holds that probable cause to remove is not the same as the imminent danger required to remove without a warrant, the line an emergency removal decision must respect.
relevance.FAIL-02: Is a California county section 1983 case applying the warrantless-removal rule and denying qualified immunity at summary judgment.
relevance.INP-12: Marks how little time pressure will excuse taking a child into protective custody before a court order issues.

cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit
cases.holding: Sitting en banc, the court overruled Doe v. Lebbos and held that social workers have absolute immunity only for the quasi-prosecutorial decision to institute dependency proceedings, not for fabricating evidence during an investigation or making false statements in a dependency petition affidavit signed under penalty of perjury.
cases.quote: as prosecutors and others investigating criminal matters have no absolute immunity for their investigatory conduct, a fortiori, social workers conducting investigations have no such immunity.

relevance.FAIL-02: Is the en banc Ninth Circuit source of the rule that a California county social worker who fabricates investigative evidence has no absolute immunity from a section 1983 suit.

cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: The Court reversed the Ninth Circuit in part, holding that Monell's 'policy or custom' requirement applies to section 1983 claims against municipalities for prospective relief as well as for damages, leaving undisturbed the Ninth Circuit's holding that the Child Abuse Central Index listing scheme denied procedural due process.
cases.quote: We conclude that Monell's holding applies to §1983 claims against municipalities for prospective relief as well as to claims for damages.

relevance.DEC-03: Is the mandatory subsequent history of the CACI due process decision relied on at this node, and it limits who can be made to answer for a substantiated listing.
relevance.FAIL-05: Requires a person challenging a stigmatizing registry listing to trace the deprivation to a county policy or custom even when only declaratory or injunctive relief is sought.
relevance.FAIL-01: Defines the municipal-liability element that must be pleaded before a court will order a county to change the practice that produced an erroneous finding.

cases.case_name: Cuff v. Grossmont Union High School District
cases.holding: The court reversed summary judgment and held that the CANRA immunity of Penal Code section 11172(a) does not shield a school employee who gave a copy of her suspected child abuse report to the children's father, a person not among the recipients the statute authorizes.
cases.quote: In other words, a mandated reporter may not be sued for making a required or authorized report to an authorized agency.

relevance.INP-01: Marks the boundary of California's mandated reporter immunity: it protects the act of reporting to an authorized agency and nothing beyond it.
relevance.INP-08: Is the California authority on a school employee's duties and exposure when she prepares and handles a suspected child abuse report about a pupil's family.
relevance.FAIL-06: Establishes that CANRA report confidentiality is enforceable in damages when an agency employee releases the report to an unauthorized person.

cases.holding: The court held that an order placing a family under informal supervision pursuant to Welfare and Institutions Code section 360(b), without declaring the child a dependent, is tantamount to a disposition and is therefore appealable, and it affirmed the juvenile court's orders on the merits.
cases.quote: We therefore construe the order of the juvenile court for informal supervision under section 360, subdivision (b) as a disposition order.

relevance.ACT-01: Is the California authority describing the section 360(b) informal supervision program, the court-adjacent route by which a family receives services without being declared dependents.
relevance.DEC-06: Confirms that a sustained petition need not produce dependency: the court may instead order agency-supervised services, and that choice is reviewable on appeal.

cases.holding: The court affirmed jurisdictional and dispositional orders entered after a mother who asked her physician for help with cocaine use was referred to the agency, holding the juvenile court did not abuse its discretion in declaring the child a dependent rather than ordering family maintenance services under section 360(b).
cases.quote: The court has broad discretion to determine what would best serve and protect the child's interest and to fashion a dispositional order in accord with this discretion.

relevance.ACT-01: Shows that voluntary, agency-supervised family maintenance under section 360(b) is a lesser alternative the court must consider but is not required to choose.
relevance.INP-05: Arose from a parent's own request to her doctor for help, and traces what happens when that self-referral reaches the child welfare agency.
relevance.INP-07: Illustrates the physician's referral of a family to the agency based on a patient's disclosure during treatment.

notes: Every case listed was retrieved from CourtListener in this session and its opinion text read; every quote was mechanically verified as an exact substring of the retrieved MAJORITY opinion after normalizing whitespace and quote marks (CourtListener's OCR uses U+201F and similar characters where the reporter prints an apostrophe). No case in this brief was taken from memory.

The existing layers.case_law.key_cases entries in the CA node files are keyword-matched noise with synthetic citations (e.g. 'California Supreme Court Case s285759 (2025)') and Justia URLs. None survived verification. Two of those titles did lead to real, on-point authority that IS included here: In re Dezi C. (docket S275578) and Guardianship of Saul H. (docket S271265). In re S.R., In re Ja.O. and In re Bradshaw were not retrievable as on-point published authority for the nodes they were attached to and are omitted.

Five California Supreme Court clusters in CourtListener carry NO reporter citation (In re Caden C., In re Isaiah W., In re Dezi C., Conservatorship of O.B., Guardianship of Saul H.). Per the citation rule these are given in slip form using the docket number read from the opinion's own caption. Their official parallel cites, for a lawyer's convenience, are In re Caden C. (2021) 11 Cal.5th 614; In re Isaiah W. (2016) 1 Cal.5th 1; In re Dezi C. (2024) 16 Cal.5th 1112; Conservatorship of O.B. (2020) 9 Cal.5th 989; Guardianship of Saul H. (2022) 13 Cal.5th 827 — but those parallel cites were NOT confirmed from a CourtListener cluster in this session and should be re-checked before filing.

CourtListener labels several Harvard-sourced California Court of Appeal clusters with the court_id 'calctapp5d' even where the deciding division was not the Fifth District. Two entries use those clusters because they are the only ones carrying reporter citations: In re M.W. (cluster 6239878) and Priscila N. v. Leonardo G. (cluster 6239227). Duplicate 'calctapp' clusters for the same opinions exist (4531594 and 4448135) but have no citations.

CourtListener stores some California Court of Appeal clusters under Westlaw-style party captions rather than the published 'In re' caption. The case_name field gives the caption as the court styles the case (e.g. 'In re Henry V.' for cluster 5809151, captioned in CourtListener as 'San Mateo County Social Services Agency v. Karla C.'; 'In re Ashly F.' for 5811798; 'In re Isabella G.' for 3195284; 'In re Marcus W.' for 2265351). Verify the caption against the official reporter before citing.

Wallis v. Spencer: the opinion read is the amended opinion reported at 202 F.3d 1126, but CourtListener records the cluster's date_filed as 1999-09-14 (the date of the original 193 F.3d 1054 opinion). The year field follows the cluster date. Many practitioners cite this case as Wallis v. Spencer, 202 F.3d 1126 (9th Cir. 2000).

Humphries v. County of Los Angeles, 554 F.3d 1170 (9th Cir. 2009) was reversed IN PART by Los Angeles County v. Humphries, 562 U.S. 29 (2010), but only on the Monell question of municipal liability for claims seeking prospective relief. The Ninth Circuit's stigma-plus due process holding relied on here was not disturbed. California has since amended its CACI grievance procedures (Pen. Code § 11169); check current statutory process before advising a client.

Greene v. Camreta, 588 F.3d 1011 (9th Cir. 2009) was retrieved and read but is NOT included: the Supreme Court in Camreta v. Greene, 563 U.S. 692 (2011) vacated the Ninth Circuit's Fourth Amendment merits holding on in-school seizures, so it is not reliable authority. Dees v. County of San Diego (9th Cir. 2020) is used instead for the school-interview question at INP-08 and DEC-02.

Calabretta v. Floyd, 189 F.3d 808 (9th Cir. 1999) — the leading circuit authority that a social worker's coerced, non-consensual entry into a home requires a warrant or exigency — was retrieved and read, but the CourtListener text of that cluster (765930 / 7078750) contains no single rule-bearing sentence in the majority that satisfies the quote constraints without truncation. It is therefore omitted rather than quoted loosely. Practitioners should cite it alongside Kirkpatrick for the home-entry question at DEC-02 and INP-10. [SUPERSEDED IN THIS PASS: Calabretta has now been added; see the addition note below.]

Haaland v. Brackeen, 599 U.S. 255 (2023) and Beltran v. Santa Clara County, 514 F.3d 906 (9th Cir. 2008) (en banc) were retrieved and read but are omitted: the CourtListener text for both contains line-break hyphenation artifacts and OCR errors inside every candidate rule sentence ('ar- gument', 'quasi-proseeutorial'), so no clean exact quote could be taken. Hardwick v. Vreeken carries the same absolute-immunity rule as Beltran and is used instead. [PARTLY SUPERSEDED IN THIS PASS: Beltran has now been added from a clean cluster; see the addition note below. Haaland v. Brackeen remains omitted.]

DEC-06 (Differential Response / Alternative Response) has no on-point published California appellate authority addressing DR/AR by name — targeted searches for 'differential response' and 'alternative response' in cal and calctapp returned zero results. The node is now supported by the federal standard (Suter v. Artist M., leaving front-end program design to state discretion), the jurisdictional threshold (In re R.T.; In re N.R.), and the closest California analogue actually on the books, section 360(b) informal supervision (In re Adam D.).

INP-04 (Court-Ordered Referral) and INP-09 (Systemic Audit / Oversight Trigger) likewise have no California case law addressing the trigger itself. They are mapped to the cases that define what the court may do once a referral produces a petition (Cynthia D., In re R.T.) and to the enforcement architecture for oversight findings (Suter, Henry A. v. Willden, DeShaney), and this gap should be disclosed to users.

The PMC-01 through PMC-06 family concerns federal monitoring, audits, citizen review panels, fatality commissions and transparency. There is no California case law on CFSR, OIG audits, CAPTA citizen review panels or the Protect Our Kids Act. Those nodes are mapped to the governing enforcement and public-access authorities actually available in California: Suter (federal standards are enforced administratively, not privately), and the California Public Records Act line (IFPTE Local 21; City of San Jose; Jacob B. for the juvenile-confidentiality limit). No federal FOIA case was retrieved; FOIA reaches federal agencies only, and requests to California county child welfare agencies proceed under the CPRA.

No published California appellate authority was located on children who go missing from foster care. Welf. & Inst. Code § 10850.4 (child fatality record disclosure) returned zero CourtListener hits in cal and calctapp; the fatality-disclosure and transparency nodes are therefore carried by B.H. v. County of San Bernardino (mandatory duty, arising from a child's death), In re Ethan C., DeShaney, Henry A. v. Willden and the CPRA cases.

In re Matthew C. (1993) 6 Cal.4th 386 was retrieved and read but omitted: its holding that findings subsumed in a setting order are reviewable on appeal from the termination order was superseded by the 1994 enactment of Welf. & Inst. Code § 366.26(l), which now requires timely writ review. Citing it for appellate timeliness would mislead. Practitioners should look to § 366.26(l) and In re Zeth S. (2003) 31 Cal.4th 396 instead — Zeth S. has now been added to this brief.

No unpublished or memorandum decisions were used. Every entry is a published opinion of the California Supreme Court, the California Court of Appeal, the Ninth Circuit, or the United States Supreme Court.

All statutory anchors in the CA node files (Pen. Code §§ 11164–11174.3 (CANRA) and Welf. & Inst. Code § 300 et seq.) are directly construed by cases in this brief: CANRA by B.H., Ferraro, Cuff, Landeros and Gonzalez; § 300(b)(1) by In re R.T. and In re N.R.; § 300(f) by In re Ethan C.; § 300(j) by In re I.J.; § 360(b) informal supervision by In re Adam D. and In re L.W.; § 361(c) removal by In re Henry V. and In re Ashly F.; § 361.3 by In re Isabella G.; § 366.21 by Tonya M. and Michael G.; § 352 by Michael G.; § 366.26 by Cynthia D., Caden C. and Celine R.; § 213.5 by Priscila N.; § 369 by In re Marcus W.; and the Cal-ICWA provisions by Isaiah W., Abbigail A., Dezi C. and C.F.

Added In re I.J., 56 Cal. 4th 766 (2013) for DEC-03, DEC-05 and INP-10: it is the leading modern California Supreme Court statement of substantial-evidence review of section 300 jurisdictional findings and of when abuse of one child supports jurisdiction over that child's siblings, a modern jurisdictional-sufficiency authority none of those three nodes previously carried. Note that Liu, J. dissented; the quote is taken from the majority's own statement of its conclusion.

Added In re N.R. (Cal. 2023) for DEC-03, DEC-05 and DEC-06: it is the current California Supreme Court law on section 300(b)(1)(D) neglect allegations, holding substance abuse needs no medical diagnosis but rejecting the 'tender years' presumption that substance abuse is prima facie evidence of inability to provide regular care. Its absence next to In re R.T. was a substantive gap. The cluster (9452179) carries no reporter citation, so the entry is in slip form; the parallel cite practitioners use is 15 Cal.5th 520, which was NOT confirmed from a CourtListener cluster in this session.

Added In re Ethan C., 54 Cal. 4th 610 (2012) for DEC-05, OUT-06 and FAIL-04: it construes section 300(f) where a parent's neglect caused another child's death, and is the only California authority in this brief linking a child fatality to dependency jurisdiction over surviving siblings.

Added Tonya M. v. Superior Court, 42 Cal. 4th 836 (2007) for ACT-02 and OUT-01: it is the California Supreme Court on how the reunification period and the reasonable-services determination are measured at a review hearing. ACT-02 previously rested on Cynthia D. and C.F. without the governing case.

Added Michael G. v. Superior Court (Cal. 2023) for ACT-02 and OUT-01: it is the current California Supreme Court authority on the consequences of a failure to provide reasonable services and on the limits of extending reunification past 18 months, including the section 352 continuance route. The cluster (9389929) carries no reporter citation, so the entry is in slip form using docket S271809 read from the opinion caption; the parallel cite practitioners use is 14 Cal.5th 609, which was NOT confirmed from a CourtListener cluster in this session.

Added In re Zeth S., 31 Cal. 4th 396 (2003) for FAIL-01 (and, in relevance, OUT-02): it governs the appellate record and the use of postjudgment evidence on review of a termination order, and this brief's own notes had recommended it in place of In re Matthew C. without ever adding it.

Added In re James F., 42 Cal. 4th 901 (2008) for FAIL-01: it supplies the harmless-versus-structural-error framework that decides most California dependency appeals, and FAIL-01 previously carried nothing on the prejudice standard.

Added Landeros v. Flood, 17 Cal. 3d 399 (1976) for INP-01, INP-07 and FAIL-04: it is the foundational California Supreme Court decision on a physician's liability for failing to diagnose and report battered child syndrome, supplying the duty side of the reporting picture where the brief previously offered only the immunity side (Ferraro).

Added Calabretta v. Floyd, 189 F.3d 808 (9th Cir. 1999) for DEC-02, INP-10 and FAIL-02: it is the governing circuit authority that a social worker's coerced, non-consensual home entry requires a warrant or exigency. The earlier pass omitted it for quoting difficulty; on re-reading cluster 765930 the sentence 'Under White, appellants' claim, that "a search warrant is not required for home investigatory visits by social workers," is simply not the law.' quotes cleanly and carries the rule, so the omission is corrected.

Added Mabe v. San Bernardino County, 237 F.3d 1101 (9th Cir. 2001) for DEC-04, FAIL-02 and INP-12: a California county case holding that probable cause sufficient to obtain a removal warrant is not the same as the imminent danger of serious bodily injury required to remove without one. It belongs alongside Rogers and Kirkpatrick.

Added Beltran v. Santa Clara County (9th Cir. 2008) (en banc) for FAIL-02: it is the en banc source, in a California county case, of the rule that social workers have no absolute immunity for fabricating investigative evidence, and it overruled Doe v. Lebbos. CITATION CAVEAT: the CourtListener cluster carrying the reporter cite 514 F.3d 906 (cluster 1385389) has OCR corruption inside every candidate rule sentence ('quasi-proseeutorial', 'investí-gations'), so the entry uses cluster 3050959 — the court's own clean slip text of the same per curiam en banc opinion, docket 05-16976 — which carries no reporter citation and is therefore given in slip form. Cite it in a filing as Beltran v. Santa Clara County, 514 F.3d 906 (9th Cir. 2008) (en banc). CourtListener records cluster 3050959's date as 2008-01-23 while the slip opinion states 'Filed January 24, 2008'; the date_decided field follows the cluster.

Added Los Angeles County v. Humphries, 562 U.S. 29 (2010) for DEC-03, FAIL-05 and FAIL-01: the Supreme Court's partial reversal of the Ninth Circuit's Humphries decision on the Monell question. It was previously discussed only in a note; any brief relying on Humphries at those nodes must carry this subsequent history in the citation itself.

Added Cuff v. Grossmont Union High School District, 221 Cal. App. 4th 582 (2013) for INP-08, INP-01 and FAIL-06: INP-08 (Educational Disclosure) previously had only one case (Dees, a school-interview seizure case) and no authority on a school employee's own reporting duties. Cuff holds that CANRA immunity protects the act of reporting to an authorized agency and does not shield onward disclosure of the report to an unauthorized person.

Added In re Adam D., 183 Cal. App. 4th 1250 (2010) for ACT-01 and DEC-06: ACT-01 (Voluntary Services) had ZERO cases in the prior node_map. Adam D. is the California authority describing section 360(b) informal supervision — services provided without the child being declared a dependent — and holding such an order appealable. CourtListener captions this cluster 'Los Angeles County Department of Children & Family Services v. Marla D.'; the published caption is In re Adam D. A duplicate cluster (2282684) carries the same reporter cite under the 'In re Adam D.' caption but was not retrieved this session.

Added In re L.W., 32 Cal. App. 5th 840 (2019) for ACT-01, INP-05 and INP-07: it arose when a mother asked her own physician for help with cocaine use and the physician referred the family to the agency, making it the closest published California authority to the self-report / guardian-request trigger, and it holds that voluntary section 360(b) family maintenance is a lesser alternative the court must consider but need not choose. CAVEAT: its jurisdictional reasoning about parental substance abuse must now be read in light of In re N.R. (Cal. 2023), which rejected the 'tender years' prima facie presumption; L.W. is relied on here only for the section 360(b) discretion point and the referral pathway. CourtListener labels this cluster court_id 'calctapp5d' although it was decided by the Second Appellate District, Division Eight — the same mislabeling noted above for In re M.W. and Priscila N.

Kaulukukui retain their other nodes rather than FAIL-02; In re Sade C. and In re Jasmon O. at OUT-02, and Lassiter at FAIL-01; Gonzalez at DEC-03 and In re Isaiah W. at INP-11 and DEC-05. Each case's relevance object still records why it matters at the additional decision points it speaks to, even where the six-case cap kept it out of that node's list.

Nodes that remain at the two-case minimum and are carried in part or in whole by the federal standard rather than by California authority, because no on-point published California case was located: INP-02 (Voluntary/Third-Party Report), INP-03 (Law-Enforcement Referral), INP-04 (Court-Ordered Referral), INP-06 (Anonymous Tip/Hotline), INP-08 (Educational Disclosure), DEC-01 (Screen-Out/Unfounded), ACT-04 (Kinship Placement), OUT-05 (Case Dismissal), PMC-03 and PMC-06. Users should be told these nodes rest on analogy and on the federal floor (DeShaney, Suter, Palmore) rather than on California decisions addressing the trigger directly.

Missing (for a later pass): In re Stephanie M. (1994) 7 Cal.4th 295, 871 P.2d 1198 — the California Supreme Court's leading decision on the section 361.3 relative placement preference and the abuse-of-discretion standard governing placement decisions. Its absence is the most serious gap in the brief: ACT-04 (Kinship Placement) currently has one genuine California case (Isabella G.) plus Palmore.

Missing (for a later pass): In re Chantal S. (1996) 13 Cal.4th 196, 921 P.2d 1229 — California Supreme Court on juvenile court exit orders and the family court's authority after dependency jurisdiction terminates. Directly fills OUT-01 and OUT-05, which currently have no authority on what happens when a case actually closes.

Missing (for a later pass): In re Drake M. (2012) 211 Cal.App.4th 754 — the source of the 'tender years' substance abuse presumption that In re N.R. rejected. A practitioner citing N.R. at DEC-03 or DEC-05 must know what N.R. disapproved; the brief cites N.R. without it.

Missing (for a later pass): In re A.R. (2021) 11 Cal.5th 234, 486 P.3d 1076 — California Supreme Court holding that a parent may obtain relief when appointed appellate counsel fails to file a timely notice of appeal from a termination order. A core FAIL-01 authority on relief from counsel error, far more apt there than Lassiter.

Missing (for a later pass): In re Christopher L. (2022) 12 Cal.5th 1063, 512 P.3d 928 — California Supreme Court on an incarcerated parent's rights to presence and counsel at jurisdiction and disposition, and the harmless-error analysis that applies. Belongs at FAIL-01 alongside In re James F.

Missing (for a later pass): In re Jesusa V. (2004) 32 Cal.4th 588, 86 P.3d 878 — California Supreme Court applying harmless-error review to statutory violations in dependency, including an incarcerated parent's absence. A standard companion to James F. at FAIL-01.

Missing (for a later pass): In re Josiah Z. (2005) 36 Cal.4th 664, 115 P.3d 1133 — California Supreme Court on appointed appellate counsel's authority in dependency appeals and protection of the child's interests on appeal. Pairs with In re Sade C. at FAIL-01 and OUT-02.

Missing (for a later pass): In re Autumn H. (1994) 27 Cal.App.4th 567 — the origin of the beneficial parental relationship 'benefit to the child' standard that In re Caden C. construed and partly reframed. OUT-02 cites Caden C. without the authority it was interpreting.

Missing (for a later pass): In re Alexandria P. (2016) 1 Cal.App.5th 331 — leading California decision on ICWA placement preferences and the 'good cause' showing required to deviate from them. INP-11 covers ICWA inquiry, membership and active efforts but has nothing on placement preference, which is ICWA's operative protection.

Missing (for a later pass): In re Elizabeth R. (1995) 35 Cal.App.4th 1774 — reunification services and the reasonable-services finding for a parent with a mental disability, including the section 352 continuance route. Fills the disability dimension missing from both ACT-02 and FAIL-05.

Missing (for a later pass): In re Angelia P. (1981) 28 Cal.3d 908, 623 P.2d 198 — California's pre-Santosky adoption of the clear and convincing standard for termination of parental rights. The California half of the standard-of-proof story that OUT-02 tells only through Santosky and Cynthia D.

Missing (for a later pass): Planned Parenthood Affiliates v. Van de Kamp (1986) 181 Cal.App.3d 245 — leading California decision on the scope of the CANRA reporting duty and what does and does not constitute reportable abuse. Would give INP-01 a scope-of-duty authority and INP-08 a genuine second case.

Missing (for a later pass): In re Nolan W. (2009) 45 Cal.4th 1217, 213 P.3d 1031 — California Supreme Court holding that contempt is not available to coerce a parent's participation in court-ordered reunification services. A direct ACT-02 authority on the limits of enforcing a service order.
